domains.name: Python Debugging
domains.description: Fix real buggy Python. Your code runs against hidden tests in a sandbox.

domains.name: Circuit Troubleshooting
domains.description: Probe DC circuits with a virtual multimeter and find the fault with Ohm's law.

skills.name: Conditional logic
skills.description: Comparison operators, boundaries, and/or, if vs elif.

worked_example.title: A boundary that is one comparison off
steps: Read the rule in the comment and write down the boundary value: 18.
Test exactly at the boundary: can_vote(18) returns False, but the rule says True.
'>' excludes the boundary and '>=' includes it. The rule says 'and over', so it includes 18.
Re-check one value on each side (17 gives False, 19 gives True) to confirm nothing else changed.

skills.name: Loop conditions
skills.description: While/for conditions, termination, guards that run in the right order.

worked_example.title: A loop that never ends
steps: A while loop stops only when its condition becomes False, so find what the condition depends on: n.
Look for any line inside the body that changes n. There is none, so the condition never changes.
Add the update that moves n toward the exit (n = n // 2).
Trace a small input by hand: n=4 goes 4, 2, 1 and stops after 2 steps.

skills.name: Off-by-one errors
skills.description: range() bounds, slice indices, first/last element handling.

worked_example.title: range() stops one early
worked_example.before:
def squares_up_to(n):
    return [i * i for i in range(1, n)]
worked_example.after:
def squares_up_to(n):
    return [i * i for i in range(1, n + 1)]
steps: range(a, b) includes a but excludes b.
List what the loop actually visits for n=3: 1, 2. The 3 is missing.
To include n, the stop value must be n + 1.
Check the edges: n=1 gives [1] and n=0 gives [].

skills.name: Function return values
skills.description: Missing returns, returning too early, using a method's return value.

worked_example.title: Printing is not returning
steps: Call the function and use the result: y = double(4). y is None.
A function without a return statement returns None. print only shows text on screen.
Replace print with return so the caller receives the value.
Also watch for list methods like .sort() and .append(): they change the list in place and return None.

skills.name: Variable scope
skills.description: Local vs global, nonlocal in closures, loop variables, shared defaults.

worked_example.title: Assigning inside a function makes a new local
worked_example.after:
score = 0

def add_point():
    global score
    score = score + 1
steps: Python decides scope when it compiles the function. Any assignment to a name makes it local.
So 'score' inside add_point is local, and reading it before it is assigned raises UnboundLocalError.
Declare 'global score' for a module variable, or 'nonlocal' for an enclosing function's variable.
Better still, pass the value in and return the new value, so no shared state is needed.

skills.name: Type errors
skills.description: str vs int, None where a value is expected, converting input.

worked_example.title: Adding text to a number
worked_example.before:
def label(item, qty):
    return item + ': ' + qty
worked_example.after:
def label(item, qty):
    return item + ': ' + str(qty)
steps: Read the error: TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str.
Find the expression that mixes types: 'item + ...' is a str and qty is an int.
Convert explicitly with str(qty), or use an f-string: f'{item}: {qty}'.
For the opposite direction, text to number, use int() or float().

skills.name: Ohm's law
skills.description: V = I x R, unit conversions (mA, k ohm).

worked_example.title: Find a current from a voltage and a resistance
worked_example.before: A 6 V battery is connected across a 300 ohm resistor. What current flows?
steps: Write Ohm's law in the form you need: I = V / R.
Put every value in base units first: 6 V and 300 ohm.
Divide: 0.02 A.
Convert to the unit asked for: 0.02 A x 1000 = 20 mA.

skills.name: Series circuits
skills.description: Resistances add, current is shared, voltage divides.

worked_example.title: A voltage divider
worked_example.before: 12 V across R1 = 1 k ohm in series with R2 = 3 k ohm. What is the voltage across R2?
worked_example.after: I = 12 / 4000 = 3 mA, so V_R2 = 3 mA x 3 k ohm = 9 V
steps: In series the total resistance is the sum: 1 k + 3 k = 4 k ohm.
The same current flows through every part: I = 12 V / 4 k ohm = 3 mA.
The voltage across each resistor is I x R: V_R2 = 3 mA x 3 k ohm = 9 V.
Check: the voltages add back to the source, 3 V + 9 V = 12 V.

skills.name: Parallel circuits
skills.description: Every branch sees the same voltage, branch currents add.

worked_example.title: Branch currents add
worked_example.before: 9 V across two parallel branches, 1 k ohm and 3 k ohm. Total current?
steps: Every parallel branch has the full 9 V across it.
Find each branch current: 9 V / 1 k ohm = 9 mA and 9 V / 3 k ohm = 3 mA.
The source supplies the sum of the branch currents: 12 mA.
Check: the equivalent resistance is 9 V / 12 mA = 750 ohm, which is less than the smallest branch, as it must be.

skills.name: Open faults
skills.description: A break in the path: no current, full voltage across the gap.

worked_example.title: Finding a break in a series loop
worked_example.before: A series loop of 9 V, R1 and R2 has no current. Which part is open?
worked_example.after: Measure across each part: the open part reads the full 9 V, the others read 0 V.
steps: No current anywhere in a series loop means there is a break somewhere in it.
With no current, a healthy resistor has no voltage drop (V = I x R = 0).
The break takes the whole source voltage, so the part reading about 9 V is the open one.
In a parallel circuit, an open branch carries 0 mA while the other branches keep working.

skills.name: Short faults
skills.description: A bypassed part: 0 V across it, higher current elsewhere.

worked_example.title: Spotting a shorted resistor
worked_example.before: Three equal 1 k ohm resistors in series on 12 V. Expected 4 V each; measured 6 V, 0 V, 6 V.
worked_example.after: The middle resistor is shorted: it reads 0 V and the current rose from 4 mA to 6 mA.
steps: Work out the healthy values first: 12 V / 3 k ohm = 4 mA, so 4 V across each resistor.
A short has nearly zero resistance, so the voltage across it is close to 0 V.
The total resistance drops, so the current rises and the remaining parts get more voltage.
In parallel, a shorted branch pulls the whole node to 0 V, so use branch currents to tell which branch it is.

skills.name: Wrong-value faults
skills.description: The circuit works but is out of spec: compute the real resistance.

worked_example.title: Working out a resistor's real value
worked_example.before: R2 is labelled 1 k ohm. You measure 7.5 V across it with 2.5 mA flowing.
worked_example.after: R2 = 7.5 V / 2.5 mA = 3 k ohm, so it is the wrong part.
steps: Measure the voltage across the suspect part and the current through it.
Apply R = V / I in base units: 7.5 / 0.0025 = 3000 ohm.
Compare with the label. A large difference means the wrong part was fitted.
Check the others too. Only one part should disagree with its label.
